newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish yields seen entering consolidation phase.
newsitem.headline: Polish yields seen entering consolidation phase.

text.p: Polish yields are expected to stay virtually flat at Monday's auction, beginning a period of stabilisation after months of rises, dealers said on Friday.

"Prices should hold relatively flat on Monday and in weeks to come, with the finance ministry keeping a lid on yields and high money market rates keeping them underpinned," said Marcin Dec, T-bill dealer at Bank Gdanski SA.

Dealers expected demand to roughly match or slightly top the ministry's 1.1 million zloty offer on Monday, with investor focus on the benchmark 52-week T-bills, whose minimum price was frozen at an extra ministry tender on Thursday at 81.85.
Dealers said, however, that banks would test higher yields on Monday, which could drive the maximum yield of the benchmark up several basis points from the previous 21.93 percent.
They said minimum prices of the 13-week and 26-week bills should hold flat at 94.76 and 81.85 percent respectively.
Dealers said foreign investors would likely bid at Monday's auction but large-scale entry, which would again drive the zloty upward against its currency basket, was unlikely.

Many foreign investors were put off from buying Polish local-currency debt because of high zloty volatility in the short-term and small prospects of a reduction of the currency's crawling peg devaluation factor, now at one percent per month.

"The crawling peg will not be cut until at least the second half of 1997, because a reduction would hurt exporters and widen the trade gap -- which is what the central bank is trying to avoid," said Wojciech Kowalczyk, dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.

During the first two months of this year, Poland's current account deficit jumped to $1.13 billion, nearly eqalling the entire 1996 gap of $1.35 billion, as imports grew four times faster than exports.

The zloty was seen trading around 3.0 or 3.1 percent from the central parity rate next week and was not expected to make any strong upward stabs without the support of large-scale foreign entry into Polish T-bills, dealers said.

"Next week may be a period of stabilisation and any large zloty gains will have to be backed up by foreign capital inflows, which are not likely," said Witold Wozniak, forex dealer at Deutsche Bank Polska SA.

Dealers said the central bank likely refrained from intervening this week, when the zloty hit a six-week high at 3.25 percent from parity, because it did not want to make Polish T-bills more attractive to speculative foreign capital.
On Friday, the zloty closed around 3.07 percent from parity, slightly stronger than last week's 3.04 percent close.
On the money market, one-day rates were expected to hold below 23 percent for most of the week with some upward potential late in the week as banks brace for monthly tax payments around April 20.
One-day rates closed the week around 22.60 percent, above the central bank's main drainage rate of 22.15 for 14-days.
